analysis.one_liner: Makes oil and gas drillers post larger cleanup bonds and funds plugging of abandoned wells.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; Congress adjourned in January 2021 with oil companies still posting cleanup bonds that, by the bill's own findings, fall far short of the actual cost of reclaiming federal wells.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would spend roughly $4.5 billion in federal oil and gas royalty revenue to plug and clean up orphaned wells on federal, state, and tribal land, and would require companies drilling on public land to post far larger cleanup guarantees — at least $75,000 per lease — replacing the low blanket bonds and self-bonding now permitted. It would also force operators to plug or reactivate wells left idle more than five years and build a public database of every federal lease's wells, operators, and cleanup assurances. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who the bill's own findings say are "often responsible" for cleaning up wells the industry walks away from, would see the biggest liability reduced. People living near abandoned wells would benefit from plugging of sites the findings call significant public health, safety, and environmental risks. State and tribal governments would receive 75% of the remediation money to clean up wells on their land, and plugging work would create reclamation jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned wells

how_it_helps.text: Creates a remediation program that funds plugging and reclamation of orphaned wells on federal, state, and tribal land, using $500 million in each of the first two years and $250 million annually through 2029 — about $4.5 billion total — drawn from the federal share of oil and gas royalties.

Raises bonding requirements for federal onshore leases: minimum assurances of $75,000 per lease or $200,000 per state, a ban on self-bonding, elimination of nationwide blanket bonds that cover all of a company's leases, and mandatory reviews of bond adequacy every five years and before any lease transfer.
Bars drillers from leaving wells idle for more than five years — they must produce, reactivate, or plug and reclaim them — and lets the government forfeit the bond of any operator that refuses.

Addresses a documented taxpayer liability: the bill's findings state the cost of reclaiming existing federal wells far exceeds the financial assurances posted, and that taxpayers are often left with the bill for wells operators abandon.

Requires a public, centralized database of every federal oil and gas lease — wells, operators, bonds, violations, and unpaid royalties — so regulators and the public can see who is responsible for what.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land would bear the cost: higher per-lease bonds, the loss of cheap blanket and self-bonding, mandatory cleanup of wells idle beyond five years, and reimbursement of federal inspection and enforcement costs. The federal treasury would also forgo about $4.5 billion of royalty revenue diverted to the cleanup program, and states would receive a smaller share of oil and gas royalties indirectly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land

drawbacks.text: The program spends public royalty revenue — money that would otherwise flow to the treasury and states — to clean up wells that private operators abandoned, effectively socializing past industry messes, though the bill directs the government to seek reimbursement from responsible parties where they can be found.

Requiring per-lease bonds and banning nationwide blanket bonding would raise compliance costs for small operators, which critics could argue accelerates industry consolidation, even though the provisions are precisely what stops companies from walking away from wells.

The funding is modest relative to the problem the bill itself documents: it cites at least 56,600 known orphaned well sites and as many as 746,000 undocumented ones nationwide, while steady-state funding is $250 million per year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is sound and the costs fall mostly on the industry rather than the public: bonds sized to actual reclamation costs, a ban on the self-bonding practice that lets companies promise instead of pay, and an end to blanket bonds that cover thousands of wells for a fraction of the cleanup bill. The main honest criticism is that the cleanup fund uses royalty dollars the public would otherwise receive to fix wells industry left behind, and that the money, while substantial, is small next to the scale of orphaned wells the bill itself documents. On balance the bill would have shifted a real, documented liability off taxpayers and onto the companies creating it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended in January 2021 with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the bill on September 22, 2020, less than six weeks before the end of the congressional session, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat, and no further action of any kind followed the referral.

The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action; the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill dead in committee and federal bonding rules for oil and gas leases unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators on federal land came out ahead: they kept the existing low bonding requirements, self-bonding, and blanket bonds, and the documented gap between cleanup costs and posted assurances remained on taxpayers' books. State and tribal governments got no cleanup funds from this bill.

for.name: Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat at referral from September 2020 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only senators who acted on the bill were its Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and the Republican-chaired committee to which it was referred took no action.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies operating on federal land
industries.note: The bill would end self-bonding and nationwide blanket bonds, require minimum assurances of $75,000 per lease and $200,000 per state, force plugging of wells idle more than five years, and charge operators for federal inspection costs. Under current practice, the bill's own findings say, the posted bonds fall far short of actual reclamation costs — leaving taxpayers to absorb the difference.

industries.industry: State and tribal governments with orphaned wells
industries.note: States and Indian tribes would receive 75% of the remediation funds to plug and reclaim orphaned wells on their land, with priority for sites posing the greatest public health and safety risks.
Requiring real financial assurances on every federal lease — with no self-bonding option — would create new demand for surety bonds, letters of credit, and certificates of deposit.

industries.industry: Oil field service and reclamation contractors
industries.note: A funded program to plug and reclaim tens of thousands of orphaned wells would generate plugging, earthmoving, and habitat restoration work; the bill's findings explicitly cite supporting jobs in remediation and reclamation.
